text: In 1835, a newspaper told New York that bat-people were living on the Moon... and New York believed it.
The paper is called The Sun.
It's two years old, it costs one penny, and it needs readers.
So a reporter named Richard Locke writes a story.
The famous astronomer Sir John Herschel, he writes, has built a giant telescope in South Africa,
and through it, he can see the Moon up close.
Day one: forests and oceans.
Day two: blue goats with a single horn.
Day four: winged people.
Like humans with bat wings, flying around... and chatting.
The whole city is talking about it.
Other papers copy the story, and soon it's spreading across Europe.
But wait... didn't anyone just ask Herschel?
You see, Herschel really is in South Africa, really studying the sky.
But in 1835, a letter to South Africa takes months.
Nobody can check.
It's like a rumor about a friend who's on vacation with no phone.
Weeks later, a rival paper exposes the whole thing.
And The Sun?
It's now the paper everyone has heard of.
Herschel spends years getting letters about bat-people he never saw, in four languages.
And Locke?
He starts signing his work: "author of the Moon hoax."
